ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
During quarantine, the FBI has been monitoring a young physicists suspicious activities. After compiling weeks worth of evidence, the FBI finally has had enough and searches his room.

The room's door is opened with a high angular velocity about its hinge. Over a very short period of time, its angular velocity increases to $\omega=8.56 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ due to the force applied at the end opposite from the hinge. For simplicity, treat the door as a uniform thin rod of length $L=1.00 \mathrm{~m}$ and mass $M=9.50 \mathrm{~kg}$. The hinge (pivot) is located at one end of the rod. Ignore gravity. At what distance from the hinge of the door is the door most likely to break? Assume that the door will break at where the bending moment is largest. (Answer in metres.)

raw_record.question_text:
During quarantine, the FBI has been monitoring a young physicists suspicious activities. After compiling weeks worth of evidence, the FBI finally has had enough and searches his room.

The room's door is opened with a high angular velocity about its hinge. Over a very short period of time, its angular velocity increases to $\omega=8.56 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ due to the force applied at the end opposite from the hinge. For simplicity, treat the door as a uniform thin rod of length $L=1.00 \mathrm{~m}$ and mass $M=9.50 \mathrm{~kg}$. The hinge (pivot) is located at one end of the rod. Ignore gravity. At what distance from the hinge of the door is the door most likely to break? Assume that the door will break at where the bending moment is largest. (Answer in metres.)

method.method_draft: Use a free-body diagram of the portion of the rod to the right of a hypothetical break section at distance x from the hinge. From the image, identify the hinge at the left end, the applied force F at the right end, and x measured from the hinge. From the text, use that the door is a uniform rod of length L and mass M, pivoted at one end, with gravity ignored. Relate the applied end force to angular acceleration by torque about the hinge: F L = I_hinge alpha = (1/3) M L^2 alpha. For the segment from x to L, include the end force F and the distributed tangential inertial force density dm * alpha r using D'Alembert's principle; ignore the centripetal term for bending because it acts along the rod and produces axial load rather than transverse bending. Write the internal bending moment at the cut as the moment of the end force minus the moment of the distributed inertial load over r in [x,L]. This gives a moment proportional to x(1 - x^2/L^2). Maximize it by differentiating with respect to x, yielding x = L/sqrt(3). With L = 1.00 m, the distance is sqrt(3)/3 m.
method.CoT_raw:
Image description: The diagram shows a horizontal rod-like door with the hinge/pivot at the left end. The angular velocity direction is indicated near the hinge. A force F is applied upward at the right end of the rod, opposite the hinge. A distance x is measured from the hinge to a hypothetical break/cut section along the rod.

Reasoning: Treat the door as a uniform rod of length L and mass M pivoted at the left end. The end force F produces angular acceleration alpha about the hinge. Taking torque about the hinge gives F L = I_hinge alpha = (1/3) M L^2 alpha, so F = (1/3) M L alpha.

Now consider the portion of the rod to the right of a hypothetical break section at distance x from the hinge. Using D'Alembert's principle, the transverse inertial force density on an element at position r is dm alpha r, with dm = (M/L) dr. The centripetal term is along the rod, so it contributes axial loading rather than transverse bending and is ignored for the bending moment.

The internal bending moment at the cut is the moment from the applied end force minus the moment from the distributed tangential inertial load:
M_b(x) = F(L - x) - integral_x^L [(M/L) alpha r](r - x) dr.
Substitute F = (1/3) M L alpha:
M_b(x) = (1/3) M L alpha (L - x) - (M alpha/L) integral_x^L r(r - x) dr.
Evaluating the integral gives
M_b(x) = (M alpha L/6) x(1 - x^2/L^2).
Thus the bending moment is proportional to x(1 - x^2/L^2). Maximize this by differentiating:
d/dx [x(1 - x^2/L^2)] = 1 - 3x^2/L^2 = 0.
Therefore x = L/sqrt(3). With L = 1.00 m, x = 1/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3)/3 m.

ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
During quarantine, the FBI has been monitoring a young physicists suspicious activities. After compiling weeks worth of evidence, the FBI finally has had enough and searches his room.

The room's door is opened with a high angular velocity about its hinge. Over a very short period of time, its angular velocity increases to $\omega=8.56 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ due to the force applied at the end opposite from the hinge. For simplicity, treat the door as a uniform thin rod of length $L=1.00 \mathrm{~m}$ and mass $M=9.50 \mathrm{~kg}$. The hinge (pivot) is located at one end of the rod. Ignore gravity. At what distance from the hinge of the door is the door most likely to break? Assume that the door will break at where the bending moment is largest. (Answer in metres.)

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The diagram shows a horizontal rod-like door with the hinge/pivot at the left end. The angular velocity direction is indicated near the hinge. A force F is applied upward at the right end of the rod, opposite the hinge. A distance x is measured from the hinge to a hypothetical break/cut section along the rod.

Reasoning: Treat the door as a uniform rod of length L and mass M pivoted at the left end. The end force F produces angular acceleration alpha about the hinge. Taking torque about the hinge gives F L = I_hinge alpha = (1/3) M L^2 alpha, so F = (1/3) M L alpha.

Now consider the portion of the rod to the right of a hypothetical break section at distance x from the hinge. Using D'Alembert's principle, the transverse inertial force density on an element at position r is dm alpha r, with dm = (M/L) dr. The centripetal term is along the rod, so it contributes axial loading rather than transverse bending and is ignored for the bending moment.

The internal bending moment at the cut is the moment from the applied end force minus the moment from the distributed tangential inertial load:
M_b(x) = F(L - x) - integral_x^L [(M/L) alpha r](r - x) dr.
Substitute F = (1/3) M L alpha:
M_b(x) = (1/3) M L alpha (L - x) - (M alpha/L) integral_x^L r(r - x) dr.
Evaluating the integral gives
M_b(x) = (M alpha L/6) x(1 - x^2/L^2).
Thus the bending moment is proportional to x(1 - x^2/L^2). Maximize this by differentiating:
d/dx [x(1 - x^2/L^2)] = 1 - 3x^2/L^2 = 0.
Therefore x = L/sqrt(3). With L = 1.00 m, x = 1/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3)/3 m.
